newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algerian bomb rips apart bus, kills 10, wounds 20.
newsitem.headline: Algerian bomb rips apart bus, kills 10, wounds 20.

text.p: Moslem fundamentalists killed 10 people and wounded more than 20 in a car bomb attack which ripped apart a passing bus in the Algerian capital on Sunday, security forces said.
It was the latest upsurge of violence ahead of a referendum which would ban parties based on religion.
"I saw the brains of someone, blown out of his head, nearby," one witness told Algiers state-run radio.

The blast, in the south Algiers suburb of Birkhadem, tore apart the coach apart taking workers to their jobs at 7.30 a.m. as it passed a school. Residents in the city centre several km (miles) away reported hearing the explosion.

Security forces, in a statement on the official news agency APS, gave no further details, other than to blame a "criminal action", an official Algerian term for Islamist rebels who for five years have sought to topple the authorities.
They made no mention of schoolchildren being among the victims. Schools generally open at 8 a.m., Sunday being the first day of the Algerian working week.
Another witness told the radio: "I saw someone lying dead near the bus, he had been blown through the window. Others lay there without their legs."

At least 40 people have been killed and 150 wounded in bomb attacks in the past month, almost exactly from the day Algerian President Liamine Zeroual announced that a referendum to change the constitution would be held on November 28.
A further 78 people, including women and children, have been slaughtered, most by having their throats cut, in three operations in the same period blamed on fundamentalist rebels.
Sunday's bomb, in an area renowned for its expensive villas, coincided with a stepped-up campaign by the government to get the electorate among Algeria's 29 million people to vote in the referendum.
Algerian state-run radio reported the bomb attack in a broadcast carrying a lengthy report on Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia's meeting in the Algiers suburb of Baraki devoted to the referendum.
The government "has chosen to come to the people in disadvantaged areas and to meet them in the places which have suffered the anguish of terrorism," he said.
His meeting was one of at least seven by ministers to explain the referendum and seek support for a heavy turnout, widely seen as essential to give credibility to the change.

Ouyahia said that while some people had called for a boycott, "the response of the people could not be more clear - this same people who went massively to the ballot box to choose frankly and sincerely Liamine Zeroual as head of the supreme magistrature".

Zeroual, appointed as head of state in January 1994, won last November's multi-party presidential election with more than seven million votes against just over two million for his nearest rival. Huge security was deployed for that vote.
The prime minister also said the authorities had devoted a budget of two billion dinars ($36 million) to spend on the capital in the year 1997.
On Sunday, prominent Algerian personalities in a published statement called for Algerians to mobilise for peace.

The statement, whose signatories included former president Ahmed Ben Bella, former ministers and others, spoke of "tens of thousands of dead, mutilated, widowed, orphaned, and political detainees, victims of the cycle of violence and repression".
More than 50,000 people are estimated to have been killed since violence erupted in 1992 after the authorities cancelled a general election dominated by Islamists.

State radio said of Sunday's bombing: "Once again this horror shows the image of Algerians, their bodies torn apart. The hour at which the blast occurred clearly aims to discourage workers who struggle to build a modern state and to sow confusion among the people at the very time when the nation needs clarity."
